articles.title: 'Dark' Creators Revisit Eerie German Forests in First 'Sonnental' Teaser
articles.summary: Lisa Vicari stars as a profiler investigating a gruesome murder in her old hometown, inspired by 'Struwwelpeter,' a real and really sinister German children's book.
articles.content:
Jantje Friese and Baran bo Odar, creators of Netflix' cult hit series Dark , are going back into those eerie German woods.

HBO Max has released the first teaser trailer for the pair's new mystery thriller, Sonnental , and it looks as Grimm as they come. Check it out the below.

The six-part series stars Lisa Vicari as Anja Vogler, a profiler sent in to investigate a gruesome murder in her old hometown. As more bodies pile up, Vogler begins to see a connection between the killings and motifs from Struwwelpeter , a sinister (and very real) German children's book meant to scare kids straight with nasty stories of what can happen if they misbehave. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Peter Kurth (Babylon Berlin) co-stars as investigator Norbert Troschitz. The regular cast includes Jan Friedrichsen as Anja’s son Max, Iris Böhm as Anja’s mother Kerstin, Merlin Rose, Maria Simon, Mišel Matičević and Stipe Erceg.

Created by Matija Dragojević, and co-written by Dragojević and Bob Konrad ( Kleo , 4 Blocks ), Sonnental is an HBO Max German original. All six episodes drop on HBO Max in March 2027.

Dark ran for three seasons on Netflix, from 2017 to 2020. Jantje Friese and Baran bo Odar's follow-up Netflix series, the ambitious period drama 1899 , was canceled after a single season.

articles.title: 99th Oscars: Every Single Contender — All 104! — for the International Feature Race
articles.summary: THR's cheat sheet of all the record-setting submissions for the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Academy Awards.
articles.content:
Roland Sejko's documentary uses archival footage, newsreels and state-produced cinema to examine how Enver Hoxha's communist regime used film as an instrument of propaganda. Tracing Albania's isolation and political transformation over four decades, the film explores how the country's official image was manufactured, controlled and disseminated by the state.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In 1993, a car crash leaves Ahmed amnesiac, so that not even his family feels familiar. His youngest son fears him and his bandaged face, while Ahmed feels uneasy about his neighbor. Yanis Koussim’s debut feature — the Arabic title means "exorcism" — reimagines the traumas of Algeria’s bloody “Black Decade” (1992–2002), a civil war between the government and Islamist rebel groups, as a horror film, blending memory, trauma and possession.

Teenage angst meets the supernatural in Laura Casabé’s coming-of-age horror film, set over a single lazy summer day in 2001, at the peak of Argentina's great depression. Amid the backdrop of social unrest, adolescent desire turns deadly in this slow-burn rage thriller, which debuted at Sundance in 2025.

Tamara Stepanyan's narrative feature debut follows Céline, a French woman who travels to Armenia to settle the affairs of her supposedly deceased husband, Arto. There she discovers that he concealed his past as a soldier and is regarded by some as a deserter. As she investigates his life, Céline encounters a country still haunted by successive wars and their unresolved consequences.

Read THR 's interview with director Tamara Stepanyan here .

Check out the trailer for the film below.

James J. Robinson's debut feature is the country's first-ever Tagalog-language submission for the Oscars. The meditative film focuses on an aging woman who questions her faith as the world crumbles around her. After a young construction worker dies under suspicious circumstances, an elderly nun whose life has been shaped by discipline, service and belief, gets drawn into a world of crime and corruption.

The trailer for First Light is below.

Sandra Hüller is everywhere in this season's awards conversation, but the German star gives her most transformative performance playing a 17th-Century woman passing as a male farmer in Markus Schleinzer's period drama. Hüller won the Best Performance trophy in Berlin for the role, which was based on hundreds of similar recorded cases throughout history. Read THR's review of Rose here .

Zaur Gasimli's historical drama follows Azerbaijani philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev and his efforts to establish Baku's first school for Muslim girls in 1901. Facing fierce opposition from religious conservatives, Taghiyev enlists the support of his young wife, Sona, in a campaign that becomes a test of his influence, diplomacy and determination to expand educational opportunities for women.

Mejbaur Rahman Sumon reimagines Adam and Eve in the monsoon-soaked Bengali countryside in this dark folk tale. A tenant farmer (Mostafizur Noor Imran) wants out of his arranged marriage to a woman (Nazifa Tushi) the villagers regard as insane. Promising her a trip to the circus, he rows her into the forest and slips away in the dark. Yet however far he takes her, the thud of a palm fruit beside their hut announces her return. Sumon’s follow-up to Hawa , Bangladesh’s 2022 Oscar submission, premiered in Rotterdam’s Tiger Competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

Lukas Dhont's queer World War I drama follows two Belgian soldiers, Pierre and Francis, who find an unexpected refuge from the brutality of the trenches in the world of theatre. Assigned to organize entertainment for their fellow troops, the men develop an increasingly intimate relationship as they put together a revue behind the front lines. Leads Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne shared the Best Actor prize at Cannes.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Check out the film's trailer below.

This Turkish-language political drama from German Academy Award nominee İlker Çatak ( The Teacher's Lounge ) qualified for Oscar submission by winning the Golden Bear for Best Film at the Berlinale. Özgü Namal and Tansu Biçer star as Derya and Aziz, a successful theatrical couple whose lives are upended after their latest production brings them into conflict with the authorities in Ankara. Dismissed from their jobs and forced to leave their home, they find their loss of professional standing and financial security puts their marriage under pressure, testing the convictions that once united them.

Read THR 's interview with Çatak here and THR 's review of Yellow Letters here.

Check out the film's trailer below.

The coming-of-age drama about tradition, ambition and choosing your own destiny follows a young woman in the Bolivian Andes who takes up the sacred ways of midwifery, but dreams of escaping to the city to become a singer. Directed by Álvaro Olmos Torrico, The Condor Daughter had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival.

A 60-something electrician has his very ordered life shattered by the sudden death of his wife. Left alone and forced to fend for himself in a strictly patriarchal society, he begins to recognize how much he took her devotion for granted. His attempts to reconnect with his estranged children are further complicated by his discovery that his son is living with another man.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Allan Deberton's queer coming-of-age drama , which debuted in Berlin as part of the Generation Kplus section, follows a 12 year-old boy growing up in a small rural community trying balance his affection and desires with the fear of rejection from his father and surrounding community.

Check out a THR interview about the film here and the trailer below.

Nearly a decade after well-received 2017 feature Western , German director Valeska Grisebach returns with another deconstruction of a male-dominated genre. This slow-burning crime thriller, set in the Bulgarian borderlands, works as a low-key arthouse take on The Godfather , as archaeologist Veska (Yana Radeva) returns to the rural community she grew up in and reconnects with old friends, getting pulled back into criminal activity. Winner of the Jury Prize in Cannes.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Check out the film's trailer below.

Majid Majidi's social drama, about Solan (Mohammad Rahimi), a poorly-paid temporary teacher in a remote, drought-stricken Iranian village was the stand out at this year's Busan Film Festival, where it won the top prize, directly qualifying it for the Oscar race. When the death of the benefactor funding the school's meal programme threatens to drive away the pupils, Solan takes matters into his own hands, turning to oil smuggling to keep the meals coming.

Check out the trailer for Midday Meal below.

Even the dead face eviction in Polen Ly’s elegiac ghost story about the cost of redevelopment in Cambodia. Thida (Savorn Serak) has watched over a movie house in Battambang since her death during the Khmer Rouge years. With the building marked for demolition, she must choose between wandering as a homeless spirit and risking the pain of another human life. She befriends Hai (Piseth Chhun), a young journalist who remembers going to the movies there as a boy. In the shuttered theater, the two watch a film together on his phone. Ly’s fiction feature debut premiered in Venice’s Biennale College Cinema program and won the Golden Hanoman, the top prize at Indonesia’s Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival.

Nchini Sylvia-Bright is back in her second Cameroon Oscar submission after Ngang Romanus' 2021 movie Hidden Dreams . In Mabanda , she plays Mojoko, a pregnant teenager who, after the death of her mother, is left alone with her abusive father, played by director Quintus, and faces rejection by her community. Shot in Cameroonian Pidgin English, it's the eighth submission by the country for the Academy Awards.

Check out the first look trailer below.

This transatlantic drama from Montreal-based director Geneviève Dulude-De Celles bowed in Berlin, where it won the Silver Bear for Best Screenplay. It centers on an art expert, Mihail, who fled Bulgaria 30 years earlier and returns to authenticate the work of Nina, an 8-year-old Bulgarian artist and possible child prodigy, whose paintings have gone viral online. As Mikhail studies her work, he is forced to confront the ghosts of his past.

Check out the trailer for Nina Rosa below.

The period mystery, the director’s second feature, premiered at Cannes. The follow-up to Martelli’s General Augusto Pinochet-era political thriller Chile ‘76is set in 1992, after Pinochet’s regime ends and a 9-year old girl is staying in an Andean ski resort where she befriends a German teenager aiming to be a competitive skier, only to vanish without a trace.

Read the THR review and an interview with Martelli .

Check out the trailer for The Meltdown below.

Chinese comedy star Shen Teng plays a chef who takes a job in Bahata, a fictional stand-in for Baghdad, to pay off his family’s debts. In this war drama loosely inspired by the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, the Chinese restaurant where he works becomes both a refuge for local orphans and a bar for American soldiers. Director Wen Muye previously made a blockbuster out of the high cost of cancer drugs in China with 2018’s Dying to Survive . This latest social drama has grossed $358.4 million worldwide , making it by far the highest-grossing entry in this year’s international feature Oscar race.

A group of misfits converging at Babel, a legendary Colombian dive bar that doubles as purgatory, and where La Flaca — the city’s Grim Reaper — presides. Here, souls gamble years of their lives with her, daring to outwit Death herself. With his feature debut, which debuted at Sundance in 2025, director Gala del Sol has created a fantastical Colombian fever dream where life and death collides and the fate of people is left to chance.

Check out the official trailer below

With her debut feature, Costa Rica’s Kim Torres has created a rural chiller, combining story combining a coming-of-age drama with supernatural and thriller elements. The film follows 13-year-old Laura, who feels suffocated by her new family, despite the lush forests and palm plantations that surround her. She soon discovers the supposed village paradise hides a shadowy secret that preys on the women living in it. Torres’ drama world premiered at San Sebastian’s New Directors sidebar in 2025.

Director Hana Jusic took inspiration from Wuthering Heights and gothic horror in this period drama, set in rural Croatia, circa 1910, to tell a surprisingly modern tale of female liberation. Teresa, a Chilean woman dressed all in black like an avenging angel, arrives in an isolated, and deeply religious community of Croatian shepherds in the early 20th century, claiming to be the widow of a local man who emigrated to South America.

Her arrival unsettles the tightly ordered society, challenging its traditional relationships and expectations. Unable to speak the language, she becomes a blank canvas for hopes and fears, particularly of the women in the community.

You can read a director interview here and watch the THR Presents interview with Hana Jusic here .

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Carlos Larrazabal’s debut feature explores the pull of home and the longing to leave. It follows Elvis, who returns to Havana after spending a decade in prison for murdering his abusive stepfather. As he reconnects with childhood sweetheart and falls back into life in the city’s criminal underworld, Elvis must decide whether to stay in the world he knows or escape Havana for a new life elsewhere.

Cyprus’ first-ever international Oscar contender is also the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis, who played the son in Yorgos Lanthimos’ Dogtooth , star as an 11-year-old and her absent, petty criminal father who returns home after a family death. The film won The World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award at Sundance.

Check out the THR's Presents interview with Myrsini Aristidou here and read an earlier interview with her here.

Prague-based filmmaker Pepa Lubojacki scoured through family photos and diary snapshots for this intimate, heart-rending look at her family's struggles with alcoholism, addiction and homelessness. The film premiered in Berlin, where it won the best documentary honor as well as the independent Caligari award.

This historical thriller from directors Yohane Dean Lengol and Hamed Mobasser is set in 1959, in the final months of Belgian colonial rule, in Club Rumba Royale, a popular nightclub where white Europeans and Congolese citizens rub shoulders as dance mixes with debates of independence. Featuring African rumba star Fally Ipupa, the feature is the first submission by DR Congo since 1997 and only the second overall.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion-winning Woman Unknown is backdropped by a Danish city free from Nazi occupation, mere months after World War II has ended. It tells the story of Marie (Volpi Cup winner Mathilde Arcel), a young nanny and housemaid about to marry her wealthy, older, and widowed employer, Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund). But Marie guards a shameful secret.

The Danish filmmaker deftly scrutinizes post-war patriotism and the era's chastisement of women and their sex lives. "There have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true,” el-Toukhy told THR ahead of Venice. "But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me."

Read THR 's interview with May el-Toukhy here.

Check out a clip from Woman Unknown below.

The second feature film from director Andrés Farías centers on Sonia (Mercedes Morales), a widow who trades her family home for a cramped apartment and finds unexpected intimacy with Aimé, a working-class Haitian man, defying her family and the racial tensions between Dominicans and Haitians. The drama played Havana, Miami and Chicago and won best film, director and actress at the 2026 Dominican Film Festival in New York.

Director Cristina Barragán, who represented Ecuador in 2016 with Alba , continues her exploration of childhood wounds in this drama starring Simone Bucio as Azucena, a woman in her 30s who approaches Julio, a teenager in a group home, played by first-time actor Francis Eddú Llumiquinga. As they spend time together, an uneasy closeness grows, changing the personal bond in ways two outsiders from different worlds, but with a shared experience of trauma, The film won the best screenplay award in the Orizzonti section at the Venice Film Festival.

The Egyptian-Austrian filmmaker Abu Bakr Shawky is back in the international Oscar race after his 2018 feature Yomeddine , also submitted for Egypt. The Stories , loosely inspired by his own parents' relationship , follows aspiring Cairo pianist Ahmed and his long-distance romance with Austrian pen pal Liz, from the 1960s through the 1980s. Starring Amir El-Masry ( The Crown ) and Valerie Pachner ( Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore ).

Read what the director said about The Stories here and then check out the trailer below.

Arturo López Rodas wrote, directed and produced this debut feature, a 60-minute drama in which three old friends reunite for a funeral after decades apart, musing on life, loss and time. It won best screenplay at the Ícaro Awards and best international feature at the Cobb International Film Festival. Vértices represents El Salvador’s first entry into Oscar’s best international feature competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

In his feature film debut, director German Golub charts the real-life story of Erika Salumäe, a track cyclist who overcomes personal and professional hardship — and the pressure of the dwindling Soviet regime — to become a two-time Olympic gold medallist in 1988 and 1992. From troubled young woman to national hero, Salumäe’s tenacity makes this biographical sports drama a story of inspiration and grit, with Estonian actress Karolin Jürise in the titular role.

Check out the trailer for Our Erika below.

Finnish filmmaker Markus Lehmusruusu (2019’s Ricky Rapper and the Strong Man ) turns to science fiction in his sophomore feature. In a future, sterile world without nature or animals, Pasi (Miro Lopperi) is a lonely and compassionate designer of synthetic pets.

When by chance he stumbles upon the last surviving squirrel, he decides to defy the very strict regulations of interaction with what little nature is left in the world and help the squirrel back into its natural habitat. Lehmusruusu tackles the intersection of humanity’s instinctive need to both survive and provide in this Fantastic Fest debut (which used real, trained squirrels over animatronics or VFX).

Check out the trailer for The Squirrel below.

The first feature film from exiled Russian dissident director Andrey Zvyagintsev ( Loveless , Leviathan ) in nearly a decade is a taut psychological thriller set in Russia shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Loosely inspired by Claude Chabrol's The Unfaithful Wife (1969) it follows a wealthy businessman caught between government demands that he recruit employees to send as cannon fodder in the war effort, and his growing suspicions that his wife is having an affair. As pressure mounts on both fronts, his carefully controlled domestic and professional life begins to unravel. Like the Russian state, he goes to extremes of violence to maintain the appearance of power and control.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Read T HR 's interview with director Andrey Zvyagintsev here .

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Levan Koguashvili's dramedy is set in a Georgian village struggling to recover from the economic upheaval following the collapse of the Soviet Union. At its center is Zuriko, a widowed hazelnut farmer trying to secure a fair price for his harvest while his debts mount. With the help of his friend Gela, he also embarks on a search for a new partner, despite the objections of his formidable former mother-in-law.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

Birgit Minichmayr plays Ella, a mother struggling to process the death of her daughter Jessie, in Sandra Wollner's drama about grief and the complicated bonds left behind. Ella begins spending time with Lux, Jessie's boyfriend, who was with her on the night she died. As the two grow closer, their relationship becomes increasingly entangled with memories of the young woman. An impulsive family holiday to Tenerife becomes an increasingly surreal attempt to escape grief and reconnect with the past.

A favorite in Cannes, where it won Best Film of the Un Certain Regard section, Everytime has been nominated for Best Film and Wollner for Best Screenplay at the 2027 European Film Awards.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Read THR 's interview with director Sandra Wollner here.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

Yannis Economides crafts a modern Greek tragedy out of the story of a businessman who devises what appears to be a foolproof scheme to save his family home from falling into the hands of a loan shark. But his plan sets a series of increasingly unpredictable events in motion, threatening to destroy the very life he is trying to preserve.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Guatemalan auteur Jayro Bustamante returns with an action-tinged drama inspired by the true story of Guatemala’s 2018 Volcán de Fuego tragedy. María Mercedes Coroy plays a volcanologist who tries to warn and evacuate Indigenous communities as a new volcano forms amid corruption and economic interests. This is Bustamante’s fourth Oscar submission, after 2015’s Ixcanul , 2019’s La Llorona (shortlisted) and Rita from 2024.

Check out the official trailer (no subtitles) below.

Snow falls on Hong Kong in Juno Mak’s underworld epic, in which a hospital bombing kills a pharmaceutical magnate and leaves his younger son with an unusual ambition for a family drug empire — to shut it all down. A long-in-the-making saga starring Asian industry heavyweights Takeshi Kaneshiro, Tony Leung Ka-fai and Louis Koo, the film premiered in Cannes and won eight Hong Kong Film Awards, including one for its score by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto.

Tony Leung Chiu-wai, Léa Seydoux and fast-rising German star Luna Wedler feature in this century-spanning contemplative drama from Hungarian auteur Ildikó Enyedi ( On Body and Soul , The Story of My Wife ). Set in three different eras — 1908, 1972, and 2020 — it follows three very different people, a pioneering female student, a lovesick young man and a Hong Kong neuroscientist who share a connection to an ancient ginkgo tree growing int the botanical garden of a German university town. Enigmatic but never self-serious, Silent Friend leavens its big ideas and visual poetry with a healthy dose of deadpan humor.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Read THR 's interview with Silent Friend star Luna Wedler here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Yrsa Roca Fannberg turns her camera on the residents and caregivers of a Reykjavík nursing home in this observational documentary about ageing and the final stages of life. Everyday activities, from dancing and exercise classes to painting nails and sharing quiet moments, become the focus of an intimate portrait of a community negotiating the realities of old age. Rather than concentrating on decline, the film finds moments of companionship, humour and pleasure in the routines of institutional life.

Check out the film's trailer below.

Set in a remote Naga village near the Myanmar border in the early 1960s, Theja Rio's debut feature follows Anghba, the community's last surviving chief. With most of the villagers having left, he remains with his ailing wife and speech-impaired son, struggling to preserve the traditions of his ancestors. The arrival of an American missionary introduces Christianity and new social customs, deepening the generational divide between father and son. The film won the Platform Award at Toronto, qualifying it for the Oscar race.

Read THR India 's review of Angh here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In Santosh Davakhar’s Marathi-language folk thriller, a young bride in rural Maharashtra plots her groom's murder during the traditional ceremony meant to bless their marriage. As the village gathers for the gondhal, an all-night ritual of devotional song and dance, Suman (Ishita Deshmukh) recruits the groom’s cousin, a former suitor, to do the killing so she can run away with one of the performers. The film won Davakhar the Silver Peacock for best director at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

Director Kamila Andini (Yuni) drew on the testimony of sexual assault survivors for this magical realist drama about the patriarchal structures of a Javanese mountain village. Putri Marino plays Pertiwi, who spent 20 years in prison for killing an accomplice to her rape at 16. She comes home to find the men who sent her away now running the village. When she meets a deaf teenage girl whose ordeal echoes her own, Pertiwi rallies her fellow outcasts to bring the abuse to light. The film premiered in Toronto, and Marino shared the best performance prize at the Singapore International Film Festival.

Babak Khajehpasha’s anti-war drama captures the lives and dreams of children and adults in Gaza against the backdrop of an ongoing conflict and crisis with Israel. The film cast child actors of Arab, Iranian, Syrian, and Lebanese backgrounds alongside Iranian performers.

Rather than depict violent battlefield scenes, the Iranian filmmaker focused on the all-too human impact of war on children as they learn fear, death and waiting are part of their everyday lives. The film also strikes a note of hope that love and life can be kept alive during horrific war and strife.

The Iraqi feature, which premiered out of competition in Venice, follows a female Kurdish sniper , Vyan, who returns to Mosul to try and rescue her younger sister. She has survived war by suppressing her emotions. When she learns that her younger sister, missing since the ISIS assault in 2014, may still be alive, she goes all out to rescue her. Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, found inspiration for the film from an encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper during the 2014 frontline battles, as female Kurdish fighters countered Islamic State attacks.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

A robbery at a rural credit union ends in tragedy, but Damian McCann's Irish-language thriller works backwards to reveal how three women became involved in the botched operation. Carrie Crowley, Bríd Brennan and Eva-Jane Gaffney star as the unlikely accomplices at the center of a story involving desperation, criminal ambition and a woman on the verge of a breakdown.

Check out the trailer for Aontas below.

The Israeli film, set in 1987, centers on a 12-year-old boy, Boaz, who while preparing for his bar mitzvah is shocked to witness his father having sex in a swimming pool locker room. The boy’s family life is upturned just as the AIDS epidemic takes hold. But a decade later, the father and his older son attempt to reconcile and accept one another.

Rosenthal’s film, titled Independence in Hebrew, premiered at Sundance and won the top best picture award at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s Academy Awards entry.

Check out the trailer for Tell Me Everything below.

Paolo Strippoli's psychological thriller is one of the rare genre romps among the mostly serious dramas in this season's international Oscar race. Jasmine Trinca plays a housewife so desperate to have the perfect family she makes a faustian bargain with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s chain-smoking stranger, triggering a series of events that, over the course of decades, will bring her family crashing down. New Line has already snatched up English remake rights to this twisty crowd pleaser.

Read THR 's review of The Spiral here .

Check out the film's trailer below.

Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s first French feature begins as a workplace drama set in a nursing home outside Paris and blossoms into a love story about two women falling for each other’s minds. Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira) asks her overstretched nurses to employ a more humane system of care for residents living with dementia. Watching a play about life in a psychiatric institution, she recognizes her own convictions in the work of its Japanese director, Mari (Tao Okamoto), who is dying of cancer.

The women connect and talk deep into the night, slipping between French and Japanese, and there’s such pleasure in their exchanges that even Mari’s impromptu whiteboard lecture on capitalism feels like a moment of deep emotional connection. Efira and Okamoto shared the best actress prize at Cannes. After winning the international feature Oscar for Drive My Car in 2022, Hamaguchi is again considered a frontrunner this season.

Read THR 's interview with All of a Sudden co-stars Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira here .

The film's official trailer is below.

Sink is a drama about a mother navigating her son’s mental health crisis — still a taboo subject in Jordan — by denying her son’s struggles and opting instead to see his emotional withdrawal and disruptive behavior at school as teenage rebellion. So the mother follows her son about with devotion, hoping her guidance at attention will prove a cure. Duraie’s debut feature, following her acclaimed short films Horizon and Give up the Ghost , had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival, nd

Abel is a shepherd living on a collective farm in Kazakhstan whose life in thrown into turmoil in the 1990s when, following the collapse of the Soviet Union, collective farms were dismantled and divided up among corrupt leaders. The aging Abel has a choice: play along for a piece of the action or stand up for what he believes is right.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Writer-director Vincho Nchogu serves up a mix of comedy and drama in her feature debut. Sarah Karei plays Star, an orphaned and unmarried 38-year-old woman in a rural village who risks losing her home unless she can prove her family lineage and claim her land deed. Along the way she has to deal with hostile neighbors, shady organizations and the promise of potential romance. Winner of the audience award at Tribeca and the Best First Feature prize at the BFI London Film Festival.

Blerta Basholli takes a coming-of-age story into the increasingly volatile atmosphere of late-1990s Kosovo. Thirteen-year-old Dua is navigating the usual uncertainties of adolescence when an incident turns her into a target within her community. Her friendship with the outspoken Maki offers a new perspective on the world around her, even as the escalating conflict threatens to overwhelm their lives.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Bekzat Pirmatov blends psychological horror, folklore and family drama in this supernatural tale about a grieving woman plagued by a recurring nightmare in which an unseen presence appears to strangle her in her sleep. Seeking an explanation, she turns to a traditional healer who discovers ominous markings on the bodies of pregnant women. Their investigation leads to the ancient Kyrgyz legend of Albarsty, a malevolent female spirit associated with pregnancy and childbirth.

A biographical sports drama from Viesturs Kairišs, who co-wrote Ulya with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, Livia Ulman, and Andris Feldmanis. The Cannes-premiering, black-and-white feature is set in rural Soviet Latvia in 1964, where Uļjana “Ulya” Semjonova’s (Kārlis Arnolds Avots) attracts the attention of basketball scouts due to her exceptional height and strength. She's pulled from farm life into elite sport in this mise-en-scène-embracing portrait of a Latvian legend.

Read THR 's interview with director Viesturs Kairišs here .

Check out THR 's portrait of Ulya star and co-screenwriter Karlis Arnolds Avots here .

Lebanon's Oscar hopeful is a heist thriller about two sisters who concoct an elaborate plan to break into a bank to steal their own money — the cash frozen by the government during the 2019 Lebanese liquidity crisis — to fund a life-saving operation. Director Rami Kodeih co-wrote the film with his wife Nora Mariana inspired by their own experience at the time, when Mariana needed surgery and their savings were inaccessible. George Clooney and Grant Heslov are executive producers for Smokehouse Pictures.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Check out a clip from the film below.

How to Divorce During the War is exactly as it sounds — a high-flying executive Marija (Zygimante Elena Jakstaite) chooses the worst possible moment to inform her struggling filmmaker husband Vytas (Marius Repsys) she wants to split up: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Vilnius-set, soul-searching drama won director Andrius Blaževičius a directing award upon its Sundance premiere.

This jump scare-heavy psychological horror from debut feature filmmaker Cyrus Neshvad (already an Oscar nominee for 2023 short The Red Suitcase ) follows a family in dire straits. With their young son not having much time left, Anne and Greg are ready to sacrifice everything to give him one last chance at salvation. But after crossing an unforgivable moral line, they find themselves trapped in a nightmare where every choice comes with an ever-higher price. Child earned its world premiere at the 2026 Raindance Film Festival.

Check out the official trailer below.

Woo Ming Jin drew on his own childhood as a twin for this coming-of-age drama about two teenage brothers in a Malaysian coastal town. At 15, Ali is the only person who understands his twin brother Amir’s way of communicating. When their father remarries, he packs the boys off to work in a salted-fish factory. But it’s their shared crush on their new English teacher (Indonesian star Dian Sastrowardoyo) that turns the brothers into rivals. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival.

Żejtune is a visually rich Maltese-language drama from the New York-based Alex Camilleri, led by Michela Farrugia as Mar. When her estranged mother passes away, Mar sees her way out of Malta by selling off her inheritance: three pieces of farmland in the countryside. On her journey to claim her land, she meets Nenu, a spirited 80-year-old singer (Nenu Borg) whose vibrant folk music pulls her into the colourful traditions of the island she’s been so eager to escape. The movie hit the festival circuit with appearances at Gothenburg and Tribeca.

Check out the film's trailer below.

David Pablos’ drama follows Veneno (Víctor Prieto), a rebellious young drifter who sleeps with truckers at roadside diners. He persuades one of his hook ups, Muñeco (Osvaldo Sánchez) to take him deep into the hyper-masculine world of long-haul trucking. The road movie, produced by Diego Luna, won best film in Venice’s Orizzonti section as well as the Queer Lion.

Read THR 's review of On The Road here .

Mongolia’s struggle to end more than two centuries of Qing rule takes the shape of an espionage thriller in Tamir Bat-Ulzii’s sweeping historical epic. The actor-director casts himself as Namnansuren, the statesman who joined forces with the Buddhist leader Bogd Khan in 1911. The conspirators seek help from Russia while building a network of spies at home. Made to mark the 115th anniversary of Mongolia’s declaration of independence, the film became one of the country's biggest local hits this year.

Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić drummed up excitement in Sundance with To Hold a Mountain , a documentary shot in the Montenegrin highlands where a shepherdess and her adopted daughter are haunted by the violent death of her mother and must defend their mountain against its transformation into a NATO military training ground. This tender, windswept feature picked up the Grand Jury Prize in Sundance and the Heart of Sarajevo in the fest’s documentary competition section.

Laïla Marrakchi offers a new spin on the familiarly-bleak tale of migrant labor and exploitation in this social realist drama, inspired by real-life cases of Moroccan women who travel to Spain to work as seasonal fruit-pickers. Her protagonist Hasna (Nisrin Erradi) is a flawed, even unlikable character doing what she needs to survive in a world where oppression and coercion are the norm. Strawberries premiered in Cannes' Un Certain Regard section.

Read THR 's interview with Laila Marrakchi here.

Abinash Bikram Shah’s debut, the first Nepali feature to screen in Cannes’ Official Selection, won the jury prize in Un Certain Regard . The richly-realized missing-person thriller follows Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama), the matriarch of a Kinnar community of trans women in rural Nepal. Pirati dreams of slipping away with the man she loves. But when one of the young women she calls her daughters vanishes on a night patrol to keep wild elephants out of the village, she puts those plans on hold to search for her.

Read THR India's interview with Abinash Bikram Shah here .

Check out the film's trailer below.

Afghan-Dutch filmmaker Dawood Hilmandi turns the camera on his own family history in this intimate documentary about war, exile and an attempt at reconciliation with his estranged father. Having fled Afghanistan and later Iran, Hilmandi has made a home in Amsterdam, but a personal loss prompts him to return to his father, an aging, authoritarian former mujahideen fighter. Together they revisit the past, travelling between Iran and Afghanistan in an effort to overcome decades of silence, inherited trauma and estrangement. The film won three prizes at IDFA, including Best First Feature and the FIPRESCI international critics award.

Check out the trailer for Paikar below.

Sisters Ade and Titi lead very different lives under the shadow of their late father. The older Ade (Bimbo Akintola) is a devout Christian and the family’s sole breadwinner, while Titi (Tosin Adeyemi) is an aspiring singer full of independent spirit. When their ailing mother comes to live with them, old resentments resurface, forcing both sisters to confront grief and the fragile bonds that hold a family together.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Kosara Mitić’s debut feature 17 , co-written by Ognjen Sviličić, arrived at this year’s Berlinale with a fierce exploration of sexual trauma and female solidarity. The movie follows seventeen-year-old Sara (Eva Kostic), who’s hiding a secret during a school trip. When the trip spirals out of control and she witnesses her friend Lina being sexually assaulted, the two girls try to break the cycle of casual violence and seal an everlasting bond between them in the process.

Read THR 's interview with 17 director Kosara Mitić here .

Hans Petter Moland adapts Knut Hamsun's Nobel Prize-winning novel about a man determined to make a life in the Norwegian wilderness. Isak arrives in the remote landscape with little more than his willingness to work the land. His relationship with Inger leads to a family and a more permanent settlement, but the couple's struggle to survive the harsh conditions is gradually complicated by the arrival of the outside world.

Check out the trailer for The Growth of the Soil below.

In August 2023, eight passengers, six of them schoolboys, found themselves dangling in a cable car 900 feet above a ravine in northern Pakistan. Mohammed Ali Naqvi pieced together what followed from cellphone and drone footage, interviews and re-creations, as army commandos and local volunteers raced to save them. The film premiered at Sundance and is the first documentary Pakistan has submitted for the international feature Oscar.

Read THR's review of Hanging by a Wire here .

Read THR 's interview with Mohammed Ali Naqvi here .

Check out the film's trailer below.

Osama is a professional photographer, and new father, living in Gaza who, at the start of the Gaza war, turns to photojournalism to support his wife and infant child. Balancing duty and hope, Ahmed Hassouna's documentary provides a cinematic portrait of resilience and humanity in wartime. The last two Oscar submission from Palestine: Palestine 36 and From Ground Zero , both made the shortlist but were not nominated.

Check out the film's trailer below.

The drama, from directors Aarón Bromley and Arturo Montenegro, is set in 1980s against backdrop of Peru’s war between the Shining Path guerrillas and the army. It follows Josué (Junior Bejar), who flees armed conflict in his Peruvian Andes village to migrate to Panama in pursuit of a boxing career and a better future.

Check out the trailer for Chichero below (no subtitles).

Narciso, a charismatic musician with rock ’n’ roll in his veins, returns to Asunción from Buenos Aires and becomes a symbol of freedom after being found dead at the height of his career. This period drama is freely inspired by the 1959 killing of radio host Bernardo Aranda, which led the Paraguay dictatorship to persecute gay men. Written, produced, directed and edited by Marcelo Martinessi, whose The Heiresses was Paraguay’s 2018 Oscar submission, Narciso won the FIPRESCI Prize for best film in Berlin's Panorama section.

Check out THR Espanol 's review of Narciso here .

The film's official trailer (without subtitles) is below.

Paolo Tizón's visceral observational doc, which premiered at Karlovy Vary, chronicles young military recruits as they as they go through gruelling training in an elite Peruvian military unit battling drug trafficking. The filmmaker spent 10 months embedded with the recruits to capture the hermetic world in his directorial debut.

Check out the trailer for Night Has Come below.

Rafael Manuel turns a sweltering day at an exclusive golf club outside Manila into a deadpan, formalist satire of the Philippine class system. As 17-year-old Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) tees up balls for the wealthy members, Manuel often frames her face between a golfer’s legs. When she ventures beyond the driving range, even sneaking a taste of a cake the guests have left untouched feels like an act of defiance. Manuel expanded his Berlin Silver Bear-winning short into this debut feature, which won a special jury award for creative vision at Sundance.

Read THR 's interview with Rafael Manuel here .

Paweł Pawlikowski, an Oscar winner for Ida (2013) and Best Director and Best International Feature nominee for Cold War (2018), returns to European history with this black-and-white drama about German writer Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his journey back to his homeland in 1949 after 16 years in exile. Accompanied by his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) Mann travels across the country, now divided into a U.S.-supported West and a Soviet-controlled East, confronting the political and personal contradictions of postwar Germany, as well as his own complicated relationship with his homeland.

Read THR 's review of Fatherland here .

Listen to THR 's Awards Chatter interview with Fatherland star Sandra Hüller here .

Check out the trailer for the film below.

At 80, Arménio is finding it increasingly difficult to live independently and is reluctantly moved into a nursing home. A former soldier who fought in Portugal's colonial war in Angola, he carries memories and prejudices that have never been fully confronted. António Ferreira's drama follows his uneasy adjustment to institutional life and his developing friendship with Hermínia, a Black caregiver whose patience and compassion challenge his assumptions about the world and his own past.

Check out the film's trailer below.

A Romanian couple's attempt to build a new life in Norway becomes the subject of a bitter cultural and ideological confrontation in Cristian Mungiu's latest drama. Lisbet and Mihai, played by Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan, are evangelical Christians whose approach to raising their children attracts the attention of local child-protection authorities. As allegations of abuse threaten to separate the family, the couple find themselves caught between their religious convictions and a state determined to intervene. Mungiu won his second Palme d'Or in Cannes this year with Fjord , and the film is an Oscar frontrunner.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Read THR 's interview with Fjord director Cristian Mungiu here .

Check out the trailer for Fjord below.

This is a double debut – director Marie Clémentine Dusabejambo's first feature and Rwanda's inaugural international Oscar entry. The drama, which explores the long road to justice and reconciliation for survivors of the Rwandan genocide won both the Caméra d’Or for best first feature and the FIPRESCI international critics Prize at Cannes.

Read THR 's review of the film here .

Read THR's interview with Marie Clémentine Dusabejambo here .

Check out a teaser for the film below.

Anas Ba-Tahaf's black comedy follows the complicated romance between a woman (Sarah Taibah, who also wrote the screenplay), convinced a generational curse will kill her on her 30th birthday, and a heart surgeon who, every operation, has to suppress his urge to kill his patients. Set in contemporary Jeddah, the film premiered at the Red Sea Film Festival last year .

Check out the trailer for ther film below.

This deeply personal documentary from director Mamadou Khouma Gueye (the title, Liti Liti, translates as "The Attachment"), is in the Guinaw-Rails neighborhood in the Senegalese capital of Dakar where the filmmaker grew up. The district is being bulldozed to make way for the Dakar Regional Express Train, leaving residents, such as the director's mother, displaced. Senegal has only ever submitted six films for the Oscars, but three of them have made the shortlist.

Check out the film's trailer below.

Nenad Pavlović directs a screenplay from Jovan Popović in the arthouse indie Wanderlust . The black-and-white, self-described avant-garde film is based on the 1957 novel Izlet by Serbian painter and film director Mica Popovic. It follows a grieving young artist who flees society to create art in absolute solitude on a deserted island, only to learn that isolation can be as imprisoning as the world he left behind.

Koh Jia Ler was a schoolboy when Anthony Chen cast him opposite Yeo Yann Yann in Ilo Ilo , Singapore's 2013 Oscar submission. In the final film of the trilogy Chen continued with Wet Season (2019), Koh plays a young man whose girlfriend is pregnant. His widowed father, a noodle seller, has fallen for a beer waitress played by Yeo. Chen’s portrait of two generations trying to build a family became the first Singaporean film selected for the Berlin International Film Festival's main competition, where it received strong reviews.

THR 's review of We Are All Strangers .

Check out the film's trailer below.

Production company Silverart describes Martin Gonda's feature debut as the highest-rated Slovak film of 2025. Inspired by true events — the displacement of the Rusyn people over the construction of the Starina reservoir — it is set in 1980 communist Czechoslovakia, where Mara (Sára Chripáková) dreams of leaving her village to study and become a pilot. But her father, a Rusyn farmer and widower, insists she stays and works the land. As the construction of the reservoir looms, Gonda depicts the struggle between tradition, identity, and the desire for freedom.

Check out the official trailer below.

Earning its world premiere at Locarno, Fantasy is from the mononymous Slovenian-Macedonian filmmaker Kukla (full name Katarina Rešek) in her feature film debut. Gender, desire and self-discovery come to the forefront in this tale of three best friends living in a fictional Slovenian industrial town. A chance encounter with Fantasy (Alina Juhart), a young transgender woman, might just change their lives for the better.

Read THR 's interview with director Kukla here .

Check out the official trailer below.

Winner of the Tiger Award at this year's Rotterdam Film Festival , this drama from co-directors Devon Delmar and Jason Jacobs tells the story of an 80-year-old Namaqualand goat herder who is in danger of losing her independence after she falls victim to a scam promising reparation for her father’s unpaid service during World War II. Jacobs cast his own grandmother to play the lead.

Read THR 's interview with Delmar here.

Check out the film's trailer below.

Eight years after Burning became the first South Korean film shortlisted for the international feature Oscar, Korean maestro Lee Chang-dong returned to Venice with a characteristically searing drama about what capitalism is doing to human dignity — and whether art has any power to critique the system that bankrolls it. Sul Kyung-gu plays an autoworker shattered by the violent end to a strike at his factory. His wife (Jeon Do-yeon) befriends a documentary filmmaker (Cho Yeo-jeong) whose tycoon husband (Zo In-sung) patiently supports her interest in workers’ rights.

Both a powerful love story and a meta-fictional exploration of the ethics of filmmaking, much of the film's drama explores the slippery line between the artist's sympathy for her subjects and the desire for a good scene. The Netflix film won Venice’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. Jeon, who previously became the first Korean to win best actress at Cannes for Lee’s Secret Sunshine , is now considered a strong contender in the lead actress Oscar race.

Read THR 's review of Possible Love .

Read THR 's interview with Lee Chang-dong .

Check out the film's trailer below.

The sweeping gay historical epic La Bola Negra won Los Javis the coveted Best Director prize in Cannes this year, immediately entering the international — and domestic — awards conversation. Weaving together three interconnected storylines from 1932, 1937, and 2017, the critic darling puts queer desire, repression and Spain’s inherited stories up on the big screen, hurling breakout stars Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau into the mainstream and potentially giving The Odyssey a run for its Best Picture money.

Read THR 's behind-the-scenes deep dive into the making of the film here .

Check out THR 's portrait of La Bola Negra breakout star Guitarricadelafuente here .

The film's official trailer is below.

Three police officers escort a prisoner across Sri Lanka’s Knuckles mountains toward the village where he grew up. The officers have reason to expect he won’t make it home alive. But it’s a long drive, and their captive proves an unexpectedly agreeable traveling companion. Lalith Rathnayake’s second feature won prizes for screenplay and cinematography in the Asian New Talent competition at the Shanghai International Film Festival. Official trailer below.

An ordinary family is crushed by economic forces beyond their control in director Visar Morina's social drama, which won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize in Sundance, qualifying it for Oscar consideration. Husband and wife Hatixhe and Shaban work a small dairy farm in rural Kosovo to support their three daughters and extended family. But when a family dispute costs them their livelihood, they are forced to move to the capital Pristina in search of work, only to find themselves struggling with low wages and the high cost of housing.

Read THR 's review of Shame and Money here .

Read THR 's interview with director Visar Morina here .

Podcaster and journalist Alex Schulman makes his feature film debut with Adult Supervision , a black comedy that allowed him to work with his once-public enemy Gustav Skarsgård. The second-born son of the Swedish family dynasty stars as anxiety-ridden Bill, who accompanies his daughter and her school friends on a remote trip, desperate to repair their icy relationship. He has help from two fellow fathers: the secretly domineering Bobo (Fares Fares) and Pontus (Linus Wahlgren), but tensions quickly escalate, and their grip on the situation begins to slip.

Read THR 's interview with Alex Schulman here .

Check out the official trailer below.

Nicolas Wadimoff has long dominated the doc and feature film space with his politically provocative work, and continues that trend with the harrowing, Venice-premiering documentary Who Is Still Alive. Described by the filmmaker as “an absolute necessity,” the project spotlights nine voices from Gaza. The group — made up of women and men, old and young — reflects on life before and during the ongoing war with Israel, outlining their neighborhoods in chalk from memory and detailing their close relationships with the friends, neighbors and family they’ve now lost.

Read THR' s interview with Nicolas Wadimoff here .

Check out the film's trailer below

Shortly after Bashar al-Assad fell in December 2024, filmmaker Tawfik Sabouni returned to Saidnaya, the prison outside Damascus known as “the other side of the sun.” A former inmate, Sabouni invited four fellow survivors back into the cells to reconstruct for his camera the brutal rituals by which they had lived. The documentary premiered in Berlin’s Panorama section and won both the critics’ and audience prizes at the Amman International Film Festival.

Check out the trailer for The Other Side of the Sun below.

In 1954, during Taiwan’s White Terror, a teenager travels alone from Chiayi to Taipei to buy back the body of her executed brother. She nearly falls into the hands of traffickers before a discharged soldier takes up her cause. Written and directed by Chen Yu-hsun ( My Missing Valentine ), the film won four Golden Horse Awards, including best narrative feature and original screenplay.

Check out the trailer for A Foggy Tale below.

Sompot Chidgasornpongse drew on the Buddhist pilgrimages of his childhood for this gently comic family road movie. When a fortune teller warns that his elderly mother may soon die, Sakol packs three generations into a van to visit nine temples in a single day. Nine is an auspicious number in Thailand, and Sakol hopes the family’s offerings to the monks will earn enough merit to prolong his mother’s life. A few stops in, Mom is too tired to get out of the van.

Produced by Chidgasornpongse’s longtime collaborator Apichatpong Weerasethakul, his fiction feature debut premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight and won directing and acting prizes in Shanghai’s Asian New Talent competition.

Check out the trailer to 9 Temples to Heaven below.

A retired civil engineer gives his Syrian caregiver money to take her two young sons to Europe. Instead, she leaves the boys with him and disappears, just as his grown children arrive for Eid al-Adha with claims of their own on the family’s resources. Tunç Davut’s family drama premiered at Turkey’s Antalya Film Festival.

Check out the trailer for Like a Limbless Tree below.

Trauma, resistance and hope loom large over Alisa Kovalenko’s Traces, which picked up the Berlinale’s audience award this year. The documentary follows the stories of six Ukrainian women — from Donbas to the Kherson region and the Kyiv area — who survived conflict-related sexual violence and torture during Russia’s aggression and refuse to remain silent.

The film's official trailer is below.

Former child star and documentarian Pegah Ahangarani charts over 40 years of turbulent political history in Iran with Rehearsals for a Revolution , crafted entirely around her own family archives. The final product, which won Ahangarani Cannes’ Golden Eye award for best documentary, is a portrait of a country shaped by political repression and in constant hope for radical change.

“I realized, 'Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,'” Ahangarani told THR about drawing inspiration from her relatives' photos, videos and voice recordings. “Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship [and] the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe.”

THR 's review of Rehearsals for a Revolution .

Read THR 's interview with Pegah Ahangarani here .

Check out the film's trailer below.

articles.title: French Court Rejects Depardieu Appeal in Rape Case
articles.summary: The French actor will stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018.
articles.content:
French star Gérard Depardieu ( Cyrano de Bergerac, Green Card) will stand trial for the alleged rape and sexual assault of actress Charlotte Arnould.

Arnould alleges that Depardieu, a friend of her father’s, raped her on two separate occasions in the summer of 2018 when she had visited his Parisian home to ask for advice. Arnould was 22 years old at the time, while Depardieu was 69.

On Thursday, a Parisian court dismissed Depardieu appeal to have the case thrown out.

Earlier this month, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a conviction in a separate case, accepting his guilt in the sexual assault of two women on the set of Jean Becker’s The Green Shutters in 2021. The court found the French actor had sexually groped two women, a production designer and an assistant director, on the set of the film and handed him an 18-month suspended sentence. An actress has accused Depardieu of rape for an alleged incident that occurred on the set of Guillaume Nicloux’s film Thalasso in 2018. We had a professional wrestler cutting off his thumb . We had a wannabe quitter scheming to try and be medically evacuated . We had a dude planting a fake idol and then accidentally finding his own fake idol. We had a woman losing her pants , a theater kid repeatedly making vampire analogies. I could go on and on about all the vibrant personalities, but with only two episodes to go in the season, it’s now becoming clear Survivor 51 might be best remembered for something else: producing one of the most dominant winners ever.

There are seven castaways left on Survivor 51 , and Sharonda is both the best connected player and the one who seems to be running the entire game. Fans have been all over her as the likely winner of the season for weeks, but this past episode in particular screamed her credentials from a helicopter in Fiji. She was given credit in very specific detail for engineering both of the last two votes, and as viewers, we’ve been told exactly where she stands with all the key players left in the game. I mean seriously, let’s just run down her relationships that have been spelled out explicitly.

She’s in a secret pact with Jelly and Devin as part of the helicopter alliance. As an audience, we have been told about this secret group since the first episode, but the remaining players still have no idea what’s going on. That alliance is clearly the main story of the season, and she is right at the center of it.

Then there’s Cristian, who we have seen Sharonda repeatedly manipulate. First he told her about Carter’s idol, then she lied and convinced him to turn on Maggie. It was only at the end of this past episode, after he watched Carter walk out the door, that he finally realized she’s not his friend. Then there’s Eric, who she straight up said she can get to do whatever she wants. I have to assume he feels the same way since he got no confessionals this week to rebut that.

We saw some tension between her and Mike this week, as she advocated for Carter being eliminated and he advocated for Thien An being eliminated. I bet you can guess who won that big showdown. Carter went home, and Mike ultimately voted with Sharonda, despite the fact that he had a final two alliance with the loveable farmer. Maybe he’ll give us a confessional next week where he explains why he went down that path, but from the perspective of the audience, it looks like she just barrelled over him and got her way.

Wait, How Many People Left Can Actually Win Survivor 51? Fans Aren’t Sure If A Survivor 51 Castaway Is Getting A Winner’s Edit Or Being Set Up For Heartbreak I Can’t Figure Out Which Survivor 51 Player Jeff Probst Was Talking About During A Pregame Interview Ordinarily, when Survivor shows us a player looking this dominant this early in the game, it’s a bad sign. It means everyone else is about to conspire to get them out because they’re such an obvious threat to win the game that they have to be eliminated. Maybe that’s what we’ll see with Sharonda, but I’m not so sure that’s going to happen this season. We’re not getting confessionals from other players about how she needs to be taken out, and there aren’t actually many people left in the game who the edit is telling us can win.

Seriously, who else can win this game right now? Jelly is definitely the other most likely contender. She’s gotten a main character edit, and we’ve heard castaways talk about how she’s a threat to win the game, but she got two total confessionals this past episode and players have repeatedly talked about getting her out during their confessionals. Devin still has an outside shot I guess. He’s this season’s leader in confessionals, but the edit has also repeatedly dunked on him for all the mistakes he has made.

I’m not saying Sharonda is for sure going to win Survivor 51 , but if she does win Survivor 51 , she is probably going to be remembered as one of the most dominant winners ever. She hasn’t had a single vote cast against her, and she’s voted correctly in every single tribal council so far, except the one where Linnea went home and multiple advantages were played . I’m not counting the Devin and Jelly vote because she’s the one who told them to play the idol and then told us, as an audience, very explicitly that she only voted against them so the rest of the tribe wouldn’t know she engineered the entire thing.

That's actually a positive for her, as is the fact that she’s formed the best relationships with the largest group of players. She also won an individual immunity idol and has gotten basically zero negative content from the edit. Seriously, what are her bad moments? I'll wait...

If Sharonda wins, it is going to look dominant, and we’re going to be talking about her in the same way we do Tony, Kim and other legends who gave us a masterclass. There’s still a long way to go, but at this point, I think it’s better than 50-50 it happens.

articles.content:
French actor Gérard Depardieu will face a criminal rape trial after an appeal from his lawyers failed.

According to Reuters , on Thursday the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that a trial would go ahead in relation to rape charges related to accusations from actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018. She alleged that in August of that year, Depardieu had raped her twice at his Paris home. He was indicted in December 2020 and has denied any wrongdoing. The International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR) Pro has unveiled the 20 projects selected for the 44th edition of its co-financing platform CineMart as well as work-in-progress showcase Darkroom and the Safe Harbour stand, for filmmakers who have experienced forced migration.

All three strands fall under the umbrella of IFFR’s Co-Production market running from January 31 to February 3, 2027.

The Cinemart selection includes upcoming films by Warwick Thornton ( The New Boy), Teona Strugar Mitevska ( Mother ), Myroslav Slaboshpytskiy ( The Tribe ), Damien Hauser ( Memory of Princess Mumbi ) and Guido Hendrikx ( Stranger in Paris). articles.summary: IMAGE COURTESY OF SUMMIT/LIONSGATE A joke from the original Twilight movie has been making the rounds ever since Robert Pattinson got cast as James Bond, and now the director has revealed that it was inspired by the way Pattinson looked on that day. In the scene, the character of Eric (Justin Chon) is announcing that the theme of the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google A joke from the original Twilight movie has been making the rounds ever since Robert Pattinson got cast as James Bond, and now the director has revealed that it was inspired by the way Pattinson looked on that day. In the scene, the character of Eric (Justin Chon) is announcing that the theme of the high school prom will be Monte Carlo, and one of the key elements will be "Bond. James Bond." The camera POV then moves to Pattinson's Edward, arriving to school in sunglasses with Kristen Stewart's Bella. On The Kyle Buchanan Show (as transcribed by Variety ), Twilight director Catherine Hardwicke revealed that the line was inspired by the way Pattinson looked in shades on set.

"That’s the one scene where I was like, ‘Let’s put the sunglasses on,'” she said. “He got out of the car and he looked so suave that he inspired the line, ‘Bond, James Bond.’ It was cool. We did think he looked like James Bond. I guess we were seeing the future." Four years later, in 2012, Pattinson said he would like to go for the role of Bond , but only when he hit the right age, saying, "It would be ridiculous to reinvent it as some young posh kid." ( Artemis Fowl tried the posh young kid approach, and proved Pattinson right.)

As the brooding, lonely vampire Edward Cullen, who falls for mortal Bella Swan but can't get intimate with her unless he turns her into a vampire too, Pattinson proved he could make masses of female fans swoon over him. Despite the competition from Taylor Lautner's abs, most of the self-professed Twi-hards were ultimately Team Edward. While The Twilight Saga proved a hit franchise on the strength of its female fan base, though, it was derided by critics and fans of more male-skewing franchises for its dedication to romance over world-building, and seemingly illogical changes to vampire mythology that had them sparkle in sunlight, and gave each one a different, X-Men like super power in addition to the immortality and blood-sucking.

Stewart had already proven her chops as a child actor, and immediately moved into more independent and artsy projects. Pattinson, on the other hand, had an uphill climb to prove to male fans that he wasn't just Edward Cullen. Working with directors like David Cronenberg and Christopher Nolan, he showed range and toughness, so that by the time he was cast as Batman, fans were only mildly skeptical, as opposed to when Michael Keaton and Ben Affleck got full-on hate. Once the movie was well-received, there was no question — if you can play Bruce Wayne, you can play James Bond. These days, it's Twilight that's being rebooted with a younger cast, and they can take on the roles without fear that they'll be typecast forever, knowing how their predecessors transcended it. (Taylor Lautner's abs are not available for comment.) Check out the full Catherine Hardwicke podcast below:

articles.summary: "I'd lost the plot," says the disgraced ex-BBC newsreader in a teaser for 'Huw Edwards - Guilty.'
articles.content:
"From trusted national figure to registered sex offender," says a voiceover in a new documentary for Channel 4 , Huw Edwards - Guilty .

The disgraced former BBC anchor is speaking publicly for the first time since the scandal that rocked Britain, letting cameras into his home over the course of a year. The film follows Edwards as he navigates his existence in the wake of grooming allegations and his 2024 conviction for making indecent images of children.

The journalist becomes the subject in a teaser released by Channel 4 on Thursday, as Edwards becomes visibly fraught while questioned. "You want me to analyze what I was doing? I mean, seriously?" Edwards asks. "I'd lost the plot." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies 'Roma' Producer Nicolás Celis, Warwick Thornton Films Set for Rotterdam Market IFFR Pro Movies Director Cédric Klapisch to Receive César Lifetime Achievement Honor

The ex-newscaster, who hosted the BBC’s flagship News at Ten program and led landmark coverage for the corporation — including the death of Queen Elizabeth II and the London 2012 Olympics — was arrested in November 2023 and charged the following July after he was found to have 41 indecent images of children sent to him by another man, a convicted pedophile, on WhatsApp. Seven of the photos were category A images, the most severe classification, two of which showed a child between seven and nine. "This was an important film to make," says director Patrick Forbes. "It’s rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues — whether it’s celebrity culture or the power of the media — as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment . ”

articles.title: NBC Is Airing Last Year’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, But Social Media Users Have A Way Better Idea
articles.summary: No parade? No problem.
articles.content:
I’ve got to be honest. I was NOT dreaming of a white Thanksgiving this week, but that’s what people in many parts of the country got. If you got up this morning wondering how to watch the 100th Annual Macy’s Day Thanksgiving Parade , you may have gotten a rude awakening: It’s not hitting the 2026 TV schedule until Saturday. NBC does have a Turkey Day solution, but honestly, it’s not the one people on the Internet want.

On Thanksgiving, NBC has opted to just throw on last year’s 99th Annual Macy’s Day Thanksgiving Parade at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones. NBC may have 99 problems, but no parade ain’t one. It’s not a bad idea really. The big balloons, c-list singers, and jazzy dance breaks are usually something most of us have on in the background anyway on this auspicious day. But social media users have a way better idea.

They later joked the lineup from 2003 “looked pretty good.” Another user had a specific year request, too, writing :

This isn't the first Macy's Day Parade controversy this season. If you'd rather go the nostalgia play, another X user even noted you can throw one of these old episodes on via YouTube, and I thank this individual for that hot tip.

It seems as if NBC’s strategy is the network doesn't want viewers to notice the parade is old, but there will be moments anyone actually paying attention to the broadcast should notice. I’m not saying that’s the world’s worst strategy given I already established a lot of us watch this while doing other tasks. Still, I think just going full in and putting on an older broadcast would be really fun, and I think would inspire people to pay closer attention and see what cultural references from the time are mentioned and what’s changed in the decades since.

articles.title: 5 Times That Doctor Doom Actually Emerged Victorious
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Comics Doctor Doom is set to make his breakout introduction into the Marvel Cinematic Universe with Avengers: Doomsday this December. Of all of Marvel Comics’ villains, Doctor Doom arguably has […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Doctor Doom is set to make his breakout introduction into the Marvel Cinematic Universe with Avengers: Doomsday this December. And if the movie’s anything like Avengers: Infinity War , then it will end on a massive cliffhanger with the Ruler of Latveria emerging victorious and leading us directly to Avengers: Secret Wars . Of all of Marvel Comics ’ villains, Doctor Doom arguably has the best track record when it comes to defeating his heroic enemies. With his mastery of science and magic, along with his tactical mind, Doom views his triumph as inevitable and some of them actually are. Even Marvel’s greatest heroes sometimes kneel before Doom's might.

These are the events where Doctor Doom undoubtedly came out on top. And even if his storylines eventually have him lose his position, the fact that he had those triumphs in the first place makes him unlike any other villain in the Marvel Universe.

One of the defining moments in Doctor Doom’s life was when he scarred his face during a college experiment. Doom wanted to create a device that would let him go to Hell and save the soul of his mother, Cynthia, from the demon Mephisto. This mission has been central to Doom’s motivations for decades. Eventually, Doom becomes so desperate that he does the unthinkable and reaches out to someone else for help. Working with Doctor Strange, the two master sorcerers battled their way through Mephisto’s demon army. However, Doom seemed to double-cross Strange by offering Strange’s soul to Mephisto in exchange for Cynthia’s, a bargain which she vehemently objected to. Yet Doom’s betrayal was all a trick, as he helped Strange escape Mephisto as well. Freed from her contract with Mephisto, Cynthia was finally allowed to find peace in Heaven. Doctor Doom might be an egomaniacal dictator, but he’ll do anything for his mother.

A huge part of Doctor Doom’s identity is that he is the ruler of the small nation of Latveria. One of the best stories that explains exactly how Doom conquered his homeland is the prequel miniseries Books of Doom , which chronicles the villain’s rise to power. After suffering a horrific childhood with his parents dying at the hands of Latveria’s corrupt elite, Doom left his home to travel the world. By the time he returned years later, he had become the armored master of sorcery and science that we all know today. With his vast power and his promise to liberate the people of Latveria from King Vladimir's tyranny, Doom inspired a revolution. Ultimately, Doom avenged his parents’ murderer by strangling Vladimir with his bare hands. As Latveria’s new ruler, Doom turned the third-world country into one of the most powerful and prosperous nations on Earth with free healthcare and education for all its citizens. Doom is a villain who truly believes he can make the world a better place, and Latveria is the best evidence of his success.

Doctor Doom is always trying to take over the world, but when he was appointed the new Sorcerer Supreme, he finally had the power to do so. Within a single day, all world leaders surrendered to Doom’s will. All nations became part of a United Latveria, and Doom allowed the world governments to remain as long as they answered to him. During his reign, Doom ended all wars, created universal health care and education, and even turned Hydra into a force for good. However, as with Doctor Doom, darkness lurked beneath this seeming utopia. Several heroes snuck into Latveria and discovered the awful truth. Doom had detained every citizen of Latveria and was draining their life forces. Once the truth was revealed, Doom’s empire came crumbling down. Ultimately, Doom would sacrifice his life to resurrect his goddaughter Valeria, who was killed during the conflict. Although his reign came to an end, Doom was Earth’s sole ruler for a time.

Taking over Earth is one thing, but Doctor Doom’s death led him to an even greater achievement: conquering Hell itself. After the events of One World Under Doom , the former ruler of Latveria and Earth was sent to Hell for his countless crimes. The “Hell’s Angel” storyline has Doom temporarily bring a comatose Captain America to Hell so they could raise a rebellion to overthrow Mephisto and free countless demons and human sinners. Doom and Captain America fought side by side against Mephisto’s loyal soldiers while inspiring rebellion wherever they went. However, during the final battle, Doom seemed to betray Captain America and let Mephisto consume the First Avenger's soul. But it was yet another trick against Mephisto. Doom had placed shards of the all-powerful weapon called the Antidivine in Captain America’s soul. When Mephisto tried to consume it, he instantly became frail and was then beaten by Doom. Thereupon, Doom forced Mephisto to make him the new King of Hell.

When the entire Marvel Multiverse was falling apart because of the Beyonders and Incursions, it wasn’t the Avengers, X-Men, or Fantastic Four who saved the day; it was Doom. As the last worlds were destroyed, Doctor Doom worked with Doctor Strange and Molecule Man to kill the omnipotent Beyonders and steal their powers. With this newfound power, God Emperor Doom gathered the last remnants of various universes and created the patchwork planet Battleworld. From his throne, Doom saved all he could, and most of Battleworld’s population looked to him as their lord and savior. The 2015 Secret Wars event also saw Doom achieve other great victories, defeating Phoenix Cyclops, Thanos, Doctor Strange, and even an Infinity Gauntlet-wielding Black Panther. Of course, Doom’s own insecurities would lead to his loss of godhood at the hands of Mr. Fantastic. Still, Doom conquered some of the multiverse's most powerful beings and saved billions of lives from multiversal collapse.

What’s your favorite Doctor Doom victory? Leave a comment below and join the conversation in the  ComicBook Forum!

Gérard Depardieu will stand trial in a criminal court on a rape charge related to accusations by actress Charlotte Arnould, after an appeal by his lawyers failed.

The Paris Court of Appeal said on Thursday that Depardieu would be tried for one part of the accusations levelled by Arnould against the actor.

The actress, whose father was an old friend of the actor, accuses Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her twice in his Paris mansion in the summer of 2018 after she went to him for acting advice.
